::: {.lede}
The brain does not wait for the incoming signal and then process it. It predicts
what is coming first and sends up only as much as the prediction got wrong. That
sentence became one of the most productive ideas in psychiatry of the last
twenty years, and the framework's most serious problem comes out of the same
sentence.
:::

The other three notes rest on these two ideas without any of them setting them
out in full, so I wrote this one to close that gap.

## What prediction error means {.k-head}

The "error" here is not error in the everyday sense. Prediction error means the
difference between what happened and what was expected, and it is the only thing
the system uses to learn.

The appeal of the idea comes from its economy. If there is a clock ticking in
your house you do not hear it, and you notice the moment it stops. The sound
reaching your ear is the same in both cases; the only thing that changes is
whether it was expected. Most of the signal arriving from your sense organs
every second is like that, already what you expected. If instead of carrying all
of it upward you carry only the difference, most of the load going to the upper
layers falls away. Set out by Friston and Kiebel through the free energy
principle, the brain is a hierarchy of estimates: each layer tells the one below
what to expect, and the one below sends back only the margin by which it was
wrong. The collective name for the framework is the Bayesian brain; the name
given to its neural implementation is predictive coding.

What follows from this runs against intuition. Perception is not something
flowing from outside in but a hypothesis built from the inside out and tested
against sensory data. Clark's review presents this as a model that gathers
perception and action under one roof, and most of its popularity comes from that
gathering power.

## What precision means {.k-head}

This is where the framework is actually of use clinically, and it is also the
part most popular accounts skip.

If the pharmacy scale shows you two hundred grams heavier, that is information.
If you see the same two hundred grams on a bathroom scale that gives a different
number every time you step on it, it means nothing. The difference is the same
difference in both cases; what changes is how seriously you take the instrument.
The brain has to make the same distinction, and it does so by giving every
signal a weight. The name of that weight is precision: how narrow an estimate
is, which is to say the inverse of its variance. What goes up is not the raw
prediction error but its precision-weighted version.

Feldman and Friston went a step further and defined attention as that weight
itself. To attend to something is to raise the precision of that channel. Seen
this way attention stops being a separate faculty and becomes a setting of the
inference.

There is also this. What has been proposed as the neural counterpart of
precision is the postsynaptic gain of cells carrying prediction error; that
proposal ties the framework to neuromodulation, and that is where it really gets
into psychiatry.

## Precision at which level {.k-head}

Because there is a hierarchy there is no single setting. The precision of
sensory evidence and the precision of prior belief stand separately, and
symptoms are tied to the ratio between them.

The proposal put forward in 2013 and still treated as a reference is Adams's:
psychotic symptoms may be different faces of one core pathology, which is the
faulty encoding of precision. Hallucinations, eye movement abnormalities, loss
of sensory attenuation and delusions are all derived from that one framework.
Where sensory attenuation sits in this picture is in [a separate
note](sensory-attenuation.qmd).

## Which direction in psychosis {.k-head}

On the canonical account, the precision of prior belief falls relative to
sensory data in psychosis, the world becomes unpredictable, and a delusion is
the story built to explain that experience.

The findings are not that orderly. Sterzer's review says so directly; some
studies find prior beliefs weakened in psychosis, others find them strengthened.
Haarsma's group showed that precision-weighting of prediction errors helps
learning in healthy people and that this is disrupted in first-episode
psychosis. On top of that, they showed it can be moved with a dopaminergic
intervention. Corlett, updating the ketamine model, accepts that there may be
more than one route.

A single study can hold both directions at once. In Benrimoh's conditioned
hallucination study, people high in hallucination proneness both give more
weight to prior belief and come out with low sensory precision. In Goodwin's
two large-sample study, psychosis-like experiences went with giving too much
weight to sensory information, which is the opposite of the canonical account.

Sterzer's review makes its own proposal, which is to put the two findings on
different floors of the same hierarchy. When the prior belief at the lower level
weakens, unfiltered prediction error climbs, and the beliefs at the upper level
stiffen to explain the excess away; so weak and strong priors can be present in
the same patient at once. Because upper association cortex carries denser
recurrent connections than lower sensory areas, a disturbance in the
excitation-inhibition balance would also be expected to hit the upper floors
harder. Benrimoh finding both directions in one study fits this reading.

But this is a reconciliation rather than a tested finding. A study that does not
say which level its task measures can neither support nor refute the
distinction, and most studies in the literature do not say.

## The same framework explains autism too {.k-head}

Van de Cruys ties autism to prediction errors being given high weight
inflexibly. Every deviation in the world carries news. None of it can be written
off as noise. Findings about executive function and theory of mind come out as
secondary consequences of this.

Note that this is the exact opposite of what is proposed for psychosis; the same
framework and the same two parameters, run in the other direction. Friston,
Lawson and Frith argued separately about what to call this and proposed reading
autism as a disturbance in beliefs about precision rather than as a weakening of
prior beliefs.

Recent tests muddy this too. Arthur and colleagues, modelling two sensorimotor
tasks, found no lasting deviation in prior beliefs or in sensory weighting in
autism; what they found was difficulty flexing the learning rate according to
volatility.

## Body and emotion {.k-head}

The fastest-growing arm of the framework looks inward rather than outward. As
Seth and Friston set it up, bodily states are governed by estimation too, and
emotion is a product of that process.

Smith's team tested this in a transdiagnostic sample. In a heartbeat task, when
the bodily signal was disturbed by breath-holding, healthy participants raised
the precision they gave the signal from the heart, while the anxiety,
depression, substance use and eating disorder groups did not. No strong
difference was found in prior beliefs, so what separated the groups was not the
belief itself but the ability to adjust the weight.

## The framework's biggest problem {.k-head}

What has been listed so far can be read as the framework's success, but the
field has for some time been thinking the opposite.

Qela's review, covering seventy-two studies, finds something in every disorder,
but the things found do not resemble each other. Mancini and Nour put it in a
single sentence, that a model with this many moving parts is hard to pin down
anywhere. Alotaibi's 2026 review asks it in the title, whether predictive coding
is a mechanistic model or a metaphorical re-description.

A framework being able to hold both a finding and its opposite usually gets
called flexibility, but looked at from the side of testability it is hard to
call it that.

This is not a reason to drop the framework. As a doctor using it in my own work,
what I would say is that the sentence "precision is disturbed in psychosis" says
nothing on its own. Without answers to at which level, in which direction, on
which task and with which symptom, the sentence fits the framework but is not
tested. When a computational finding can answer those is in the [HGF
note](hierarchical-gaussian-filter.qmd); the same problem in the schizophrenia
literature is in the [belief updating note](belief-updating-in-psychosis.qmd).
